newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil seeks order amid police strike violence.
newsitem.headline: Brazil seeks order amid police strike violence.

text.p: Brazil's minister of justice on Wednesday said mutinous civil and military police have gone too far in strikes and protests demanding better pay and conditions.

"Protesting with your gun in your hand is not a way to pressure the government over salaries. That's not pressure, that's aggression. It's gone beyond all limits," a spokeswoman quoted Justice Minister Iris Rezende as saying.
President Fernando Henrique Cardoso has also demanded action, presidency officials said.
"The lack of pay does not justify indiscipline," Cardoso said while visiting Sao Paulo on Tuesday.
Protests by police demanding salary increases have spread through more than a dozen of Brazil's 27 states since they began in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state, last month.
In Belo Horizonte, an officer died after being shot in a clash between striking civil police and on-duty military police, which despite their name are not part of the armed forces.
Two weeks ago, three people were injured when strikers traded shots with troops in the northeastern state of Alagoas.

And on Tuesday, up to five people were injured during a street battle between police protesters and a special military police unit in Fortaleza, capital of Ceara state, also in Brazil's poverty-stricken northeast.
"We are going to maintain security no matter the cost," said Ivandro Alves de Souza, civil police chief in Fortaleza.
"To strive for justifiable pay demands is okay. But it's not okay to set out on an armed struggle that threatens the safety of the population," Souza told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Newspapers reported that three banks were robbed while civil and military police were trading shots on Tuesday in the centre of Fortaleza. Troops have been called out to maintain order.
Cardoso has summoned top security officials to Brasilia next week to discuss the strike, which has exposed the fragility of Brazil's creaking public security apparatus.
Salaries are so poor that officers frequently turn to crime to make ends meet, working as bodyguards at night for the drug traffickers they hunt during the day.
Cardoso said the strikes highlighted the need for a drastic reform of Brazil's multi-tiered police service.
"What we have seen in the last few days cannot take place in a country with a degree of democracy and progress," he said.
